Summary: Deuteronomy 23:7 forbids abhorring an Egyptian: 'because thou wast a stranger in his land.' Egypt enslaved Israel, yet the sojourn itself — shelter in famine — is remembered against abhorrence.
Commandment: Do not abhor an Egyptian, because you were a stranger in his land.
Application: Memory cuts both ways: Egypt's oppression is remembered, and so is Egypt's shelter. Abhorrence is refused even toward a former oppressor, and their children of the third generation may enter the assembly. Debated: how far these assembly-admission provisions carry into the church is genuinely disputed — this row does not settle it.
Purpose: To protect the weaker party at each family step (Deuteronomy 21-25). Debated: the divorce certificate is read by Jesus as concession to hardness of heart, not God's design (Matthew 19:8), and levirate marriage ended, while creation marriage itself is reaffirmed. The site does not settle a single duration for this cluster because its parts do not share one fate.
